title: Does makeup invalidate wudu and ghusl?
headline: Makeup blocks wudu and ghusl only when it forms a water-resistant layer over the skin

summary.text: The four schools agree that a barrier preventing water from reaching the skin invalidates wudu and ghusl, while a product that leaves only colour, or that water penetrates, does not. Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali books all condition validity on the absence of a barrier, though they phrase it differently and differ on small or unavoidable traces. Recent fatwas from Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyyah, Darul Iftaa Jordan, IslamQA, Ibn Baz and Ibn Uthaymeen apply the same test: a layering cosmetic must be removed, a colouring one need not.

paragraphs.text: The wudu verse commands washing the face and the other limbs, and jurists read washing as water reaching the skin itself. The same verse closes with "Allah does not intend to make difficulty for you," which jurists used both to insist on full washing and to grant concessions where a barrier cannot realistically be removed.

For ghusl the Quran uses the expression "until you have washed your whole body," and the schools applied the same logic: al-Bahuti defines valid ghusl as one in which a person removes anything that prevents water reaching the skin. The Quran also praises "those who purify themselves," the general virtue the rulings serve rather than a technical rule about cosmetics.

A man performed wudu and left a spot the size of a nail on his foot, and the Prophet ﷺ said, "Go back and perform your ablution properly" (Sahih Muslim 243). A second version adds the prayer: a Companion saw a man praying with a dirham-sized spot on his foot that water had not reached, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to repeat the wudu and the prayer (Sunan Abi Dawud 175, graded sahih by al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai, sahih li-ghayrihi by Shu'ayb al-Arnaut), and Imam Ahmad called its chain good. The same content comes through Ibn Majah from Umar and from Anas, a report graded sahih.

One report cuts the other way: Ali narrates that a man found a fingernail-sized dry spot after ghusl, and the Prophet ﷺ said, "If you had wiped over it with your hand, that would have been enough for you." Al-Albani graded it very weak, and Muhammad Fuad Abd al-Baqi, Shu'ayb al-Arnaut and Zubair Ali Zai all graded it weak (Sunan Ibn Majah 664).

The positive command to make water reach everywhere is in the hadith of Laqit ibn Sabirah: "Perform ablution thoroughly, pass your fingers through the spaces between your fingers, and sniff water up into the nose deeply, unless you are fasting" (Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, who called it hasan sahih). At-Tirmidhi's own grading of the shorter version is hasan sahih, and Ibn Majah's version is graded sahih. The link to prayer is stated plainly: "Allah does not accept prayer without purification" (Sunan Ibn Majah 271, sahih).

The Hanafis list among the conditions of wudu "the whole skin being reached by purifying water… and the removal of what prevents water reaching the body, because a barrier is forbidden, such as wax and fat," and even a needle's-point dry area voids it; al-Fatawa al-Hindiyya repeats the needle-point rule. Ibn Abidin records the fatwa that henna, even with substance, does not prevent wudu because water penetrates it, and he reports the objection to that reasoning and answers it with necessity. Maraqi al-Falah excuses nail dirt and a dyer's dye out of necessity.

The Malikis, in al-Dardir's al-Sharh al-Saghir, list among the conditions "the absence of a barrier preventing water from the skin, such as wax or congealed grease," and al-Sawi notes that oil which water cuts through and does not remain is harmless; al-Dasuqi says only dirt that has solidified like clay must be removed. 'Illaysh in Manh al-Jalil names wax, pitch, ink and dirt that block water, while a ring that water passes under need not be removed. The Malikis are also the school that does not require moving a permitted ring.

Al-Nawawi in al-Majmu' says: "If there is on some of his limbs wax, dough, henna or the like and it prevents water reaching any part of the limb, his purification is not valid," but if only the colour or trace of henna or a flowing oil remains and water reaches and runs over the skin, it is valid. Mughni al-Muhtaj lists "the absence of a barrier" among the conditions of both wudu and ghusl. Darul Iftaa Jordan, a Shafi'i body, says most modern makeup is of the colour type and therefore affects neither wudu nor ghusl.

Al-Mardawi in al-Insaf lists among the conditions "removing what prevents water reaching the limb"; al-Rawd al-Murbi' states the same. Al-Mughni reports Ibn Aqil's strict view that dirt under the nails must go, against the view that habitual dirt is excused because the Prophet ﷺ would have clarified it. Ibn Taymiyyah's position, recorded in al-Insaf and Kashshaf al-Qina', forgives any small barrier anywhere on the body, by analogy with dirt under the nail.

The sharpest tension is between the sahih command to repeat wudu over a fingernail-sized dry spot and the concession for small unavoidable traces. Scholars reconciled it by noting that the man in the hadith had simply failed to wash part of the limb, which he could easily have done, whereas the concession covers what habitually cannot be avoided and would have been clarified had it invalidated worship, a reasoning al-Bahuti states explicitly and Dar al-Ifta summarises under the maxim that hardship brings ease.

The weak report that wiping with the hand would have sufficed would have supported leniency, but because al-Albani and others graded it very weak, it cannot carry the weight of the sahih reports; that is why the schools did not build the ruling on it.

The Hanafi treatment of henna looks inconsistent with the Hanafi needle-point rule, and Ibn Abidin addresses exactly that: the general reasoning is that water penetrates henna because it lacks stickiness and solidity, and where that is disputed the fatwa rests on necessity for dyers and similar workers. This is a case of a school qualifying its own general principle rather than denying it.

The apparent split over whether makeup invalidates anything at all dissolves once the object is identified: a layer with mass that survives water versus a colour or an absorbed product. Applying makeup after a valid wudu is a separate matter, and the Egyptian fatwa is explicit that it does not break the wudu; the question only arises at the next purification. Where removal itself harms the skin, the barrier is treated like a splint rather than a reason to abandon purification, but tayammum is not a licence to keep makeup on when it can be washed off.

Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyyah answered in 2004 (Mufti Ali Gomaa, fatwa 1916) that cosmetics which stop water reaching hair or skin must be removed before wudu, and those that do not are not obligatory to remove. Its 1984 fatwa (3380) adds that nail polish and face cream do not break a wudu already made, but they must be removed before starting a fresh wudu, since the polish is an insulating layer over the nail and the cream a greasy film over the skin. The same house defines the barrier as whatever is solid or congealed, like wax, grease or dough, as opposed to liquids, creams, moisturisers, or henna whose substance is gone and only colour remains, and it refuses to let a woman resort to tayammum simply because she is wearing makeup, unless using water would cause real harm.

Darul Iftaa Jordan (2022) divides cosmetics into a layering type, which voids wudu and ghusl and must be removed, and a colouring type like henna, which "is probably the case with most types of makeup," so it affects neither. IslamQA's answers follow the same test: a barrier is a substance with mass that is water-resistant and does not dissolve, while powder and similar products need only be rubbed well so water is thought to reach the skin; the 2006 answer states that if it is merely colour, or so slight that it does not block water, the wudu is valid. A later IslamQA answer (2026) extends the ruling on hardship: waterproof camouflage dye for vitiligo, hard to remove at every wudu, takes the ruling of the splint (jabirah), so one washes the sound area and wipes over the covered part.

Ibn Baz drew the same line, requiring removal of anything with a body that blocks water whether on face, arm or leg, and allowing a dye with no layer; asked about someone who prayed for months unaware, he limited the repetition to the current prayer, comparing it to the Bedouin the Prophet ﷺ taught and the woman with irregular bleeding, and did not require years of past prayers. Ibn Uthaymeen required removal of solid ointments but not non-solid ones, while recommending rubbing the area so water does not simply slide off, and he acknowledged that Ibn Taymiyyah was lenient about small barriers while others required removal even of a ring or less. Among Hanafi muftis online, waterproof and water-resistant mascara and eyeliner are treated alike as blocking water, while porous glitter particles are considered not to block it.
